nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder, with a documented stressor and ongoing symptom severity to Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (stress-induced cardiomyopathy with residual or recurrent left ventricular dysfunction) in a veteran with service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder; individual attribution is not established.

Neuroendocrine-to-myocardial sequence: post-traumatic stress disorder is characterized by sustained sympathetic overactivity with elevated circulating catecholamines, blunted vagal tone, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis dysregulation, which leaves the myocardium primed for an exaggerated response to an acute stressor. During such an episode, a catecholamine surge acts on apical myocardial beta-receptors and produces a signaling switch from Gs to Gi-mediated pathways, together with microvascular spasm, calcium-handling disturbance, and acute energy failure from supraphysiologic fatty-acid loading; the result is apical akinesis with basal hyperkinesis — the classic takotsubo pattern — in the absence of obstructive coronary disease. The dysfunction resolves in most patients within days to weeks, but a minority have persistent ventricular impairment, and recurrence occurs in a clinically meaningful proportion, which is the basis on which a chronic disability may be claimed. Nayeri et al. (PMID 29544664) reviewed psychiatric illness in takotsubo cardiomyopathy and concluded that there is a strong association between pre-existing psychiatric illness, particularly anxiety and mood spectrum disorders, and takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Lazzeroni et al. (PMID 29168538) compared 58 takotsubo patients with and without pre-existing anxiety disorders and found that a substantial share (31 of 58) had a prior history of anxiety disorders, with the exclusively emotional stressful event rate higher in patients with anxiety disorders. Gonuguntla et al. (PMID 38331372) analyzed the National Inpatient Sample and Nationwide Readmissions Database for 2016 through 2018 and found psychiatric disorders documented in up to 43 percent of takotsubo patients, while examining whether psychiatric comorbidity altered outcomes. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder is asserted to have produced a discrete cardiac disease, stress cardiomyopathy, with its own diagnostic code at DC 7020 rather than being folded into the psychiatric evaluation. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory, because the literature describes a new acute cardiac event in a previously unaffected ventricle rather than measurable worsening of an existing structural heart disease; aggravation would govern only where the record documents pre-existing cardiomyopathy or coronary disease and the claim is that the stress-mediated episodes worsened a baseline ventricular dysfunction, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require: the diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder with its documented stressor; an acute coronary syndrome evaluation that excluded obstructive coronary disease; imaging documentation of the characteristic apical ballooning pattern with reduced ejection fraction; a documented emotional or psychological trigger temporally proximate to the episode; and, for a compensable rating, serial echocardiographic evidence of persistent or recurrent left ventricular dysfunction. Only then can an examiner state that the takotsubo cardiomyopathy and any residual dysfunction are at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected post-traumatic stress disorder — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Two candid limitations must be disclosed. First, the cited literature concerns psychiatric illness broadly — principally anxiety and mood spectrum disorders — and PTSD-specific data are comparatively limited, so the association cannot be treated as PTSD-specific without individual evidence linking the episodes to PTSD symptoms. Second, takotsubo cardiomyopathy is characteristically transient, so a claim that rests only on a resolved acute episode will fail for lack of residual disability rather than for lack of causation. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include acute coronary syndrome and spontaneous coronary artery dissection, pheochromocytoma and other catecholamine-secreting tumors, sepsis and critical illness, subarachnoid hemorrhage and other acute intracranial events, thyrotoxicosis, cocaine and stimulant use, alcohol withdrawal, perioperative stress, and chemotherapy including fluoropyrimidines and checkpoint inhibitors. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: a cardiac rating under DC 7020 may not be combined with a second evaluation for the same heart failure symptoms under another heart code, and the psychiatric rating under § 4.130 must not be used to compensate the same limitation of daily functioning that the cardiac evaluation represents.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Rheumatoid arthritis (service-connected), on chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy to Posterior subcapsular cataract (corticosteroid-induced); individual attribution is not established.

Systemic glucocorticoid therapy causes a characteristic posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC) through direct, receptor-mediated effects on the lens epithelium. Aqueous glucocorticoid reaches the lens and binds glucocorticoid receptors in epithelial cells at the anterior equator; the resulting changes in epithelial proliferation, migration, and differentiation disturb the orderly formation of lens fibers beneath the posterior capsule, where aberrant cells and disorganized crystallins accumulate. Biochemical correlates include altered crystallin expression and aggregation, disturbed ion and water transport with hydration of lens fibers, oxidative stress, and impaired antioxidant defenses; the opacities begin at the posterior pole, are typically bilateral, and may progress with continued exposure. Risk is related to dose, duration, and individual susceptibility (potency and route matter), and concurrent hyperglycemia may amplify lens damage. Quantitatively, in a 10-year population-based cohort of 3,654 adults with photographic lens grading, current users of oral corticosteroids had a substantially increased risk of incident posterior subcapsular cataract (odds ratio 4.11, 95% CI 1.67-10.08) and nuclear cataract (OR 3.45, 95% CI 1.26-9.43), with no increased cortical cataract risk; users of both inhaled and oral corticosteroids had an adjusted odds ratio of 4.76 (95% CI 2.59-8.74) for PSC cataract. A systematic literature review of 32 studies of long-term systemic corticosteroid exposure lists cataract (1-3% prevalence) among the common toxicities, alongside fracture (21-30%), hypertension (more than 30%), and gastrointestinal and metabolic adverse events, and notes that dose-duration risk relationships remain poorly quantified. The classic literature review documents the well-established association between corticosteroid therapy and posterior subcapsular cataract while cautioning that published series do not establish a simple dose-threshold relationship because of individual lens susceptibility. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so a visually significant PSC cataract developing on documented chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where a pre-existing cataract is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the systemic corticosteroid regimen (drug, prednisone-equivalent daily dose, cumulative duration, dates), the lens findings with slit-lamp or photographic documentation and posterior subcapsular morphology, the chronology of steroid exposure relative to opacity development, and the measured visual effect; exclude or account for age-related nuclear or cortical cataract (the subtype not associated with steroids in the cohort above), diabetes, smoking, ultraviolet exposure, ocular trauma, uveitis or intraocular inflammation, and prior ocular surgery.

Risk is related to dose, duration, and individual susceptibility (potency and route matter), and concurrent hyperglycemia may amplify lens damage. Quantitatively, in a 10-year population-based cohort of 3,654 adults with photographic lens grading, current users of oral corticosteroids had a substantially increased risk of incident posterior subcapsular cataract (odds ratio 4.11, 95% CI 1.67-10.08) and nuclear cataract (OR 3.45, 95% CI 1.26-9.43), with no increased cortical cataract risk; users of both inhaled and oral corticosteroids had an adjusted odds ratio of 4.76 (95% CI 2.59-8.74) for PSC cataract. A systematic literature review of 32 studies of long-term systemic corticosteroid exposure lists cataract (1-3% prevalence) among the common toxicities, alongside fracture (21-30%), hypertension (more than 30%), and gastrointestinal and metabolic adverse events, and notes that dose-duration risk relationships remain poorly quantified. The classic literature review documents the well-established association between corticosteroid therapy and posterior subcapsular cataract while cautioning that published series do not establish a simple dose-threshold relationship because of individual lens susceptibility. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so a visually significant PSC cataract developing on documented chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where a pre-existing cataract is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Rheumatoid arthritis (service-connected), on chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy to Osteopenia (glucocorticoid-induced bone loss); individual attribution is not established.

Systemic glucocorticoids produce bone loss through direct effects on bone cells and bone vascularity, and the risk appears early in treatment. Glucocorticoids reduce the lifespan and function of osteoblasts and osteocytes, shift bone remodeling toward resorption, suppress gonadal and growth-hormone axes, and reduce bone vascularity, so that bone strength falls more than bone mineral density alone would predict; trabecular-rich sites such as the vertebrae and femoral neck are affected disproportionately, and bone loss is fastest in the first months of therapy. The fracture risk is dose-dependent and detectable even at low doses and with short courses, which matters for veterans treated with repeated steroid bursts for a service-connected inflammatory condition. Quantitatively, a cohort of 244,235 oral corticosteroid users matched to 244,235 controls found dose-dependent fracture risk: relative rate of hip fracture 0.99 (95% CI 0.82-1.20) at prednisolone doses under 2.5 mg/day, rising to 1.77 (1.55-2.02) at 2.5-7.5 mg/day and 2.27 (1.94-2.66) at 7.5 mg/day or more; vertebral fracture rates rose in parallel from 1.55 to 2.59 to 5.18; and a nationwide cohort of 1,548,945 adults found that 21.1% received short-term oral corticosteroids and that fracture risk was increased within 30 days of initiation (incidence rate ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.69-2.07), persisting at prednisone-equivalent doses below 20 mg/day. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so glucocorticoid-induced osteopenia (reduced bone mineral density and/or fragility fracture) developing on documented systemic corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where reduced bone density predates the steroid exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the steroid regimen (drug, prednisone-equivalent dose, duration, cumulative exposure, dates), dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry results with T-scores and dates, fracture history with imaging, and the chronology of exposure relative to bone loss; and address competing causes — postmenopausal and age-related bone loss, hypogonadism, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D and calcium deficiency, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, smoking, alcohol, other medications (proton-pump inhibitors, anticonvulsants, aromatase inhibitors), and immobilization. The rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20 to DC 5013 because no code specifically addresses osteopenia.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Rheumatoid arthritis (service-connected), on chronic corticosteroid therapy (systemic, topical ocular, periocular, or inhaled) to Glaucoma (corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension progressing to secondary open-angle glaucoma); individual attribution is not established.

Corticosteroids raise intraocular pressure and produce secondary open-angle glaucoma by increasing resistance to aqueous humor outflow through the conventional pathway — the trabecular meshwork, the juxtacanalicular connective tissue, and the inner wall of the Schlemm canal. Glucocorticoids induce extracellular matrix deposition (including myocilin and fibronectin) and cytoskeletal changes in trabecular meshwork cells that reduce outflow facility, so intraocular pressure rises; in susceptible individuals the steroid response progresses from asymptomatic ocular hypertension to sustained pressure elevation, glaucomatous optic neuropathy, and irreversible visual-field loss if the elevation is unrecognized or continues. The effect is a class property of corticosteroids rather than of any one drug or route: it has been recognized since the 1950s after systemic ACTH and both topical and systemic corticosteroids, risk increases with prolonged use, higher frequency, higher anti-inflammatory potency, and greater ocular penetrance (and is greater in children and in known steroid responders), and reducing the molecule's intrinsic steroid activity (as with loteprednol etabonate) demonstrably reduces the intraocular pressure effect. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension and glaucomatous damage developing on documented corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where pre-existing open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension is documented before steroid exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the corticosteroid regimen (drug, route, potency, frequency, duration, dates — including topical ocular and periocular injections, which carry the highest ocular risk), serial intraocular pressure measurements and optic-nerve and visual-field examinations with dates, the chronology of pressure rise relative to steroid exposure, and the response to steroid withdrawal or pressure-lowering therapy; and address competing causes — primary open-angle glaucoma (family history, age, myopia, African ancestry, diabetes), angle-closure mechanisms, uveitis and other intraocular inflammation, pseudoexfoliation, and pigment dispersion. Because the diagnosis is open-angle glaucoma unless the mechanism is angle closure, the claim is evaluated under DC 6013 (or DC 6012 for angle closure) — the requirement for a diagnostic code is met directly rather than by analogy.

Proposed route from Service-connected rheumatoid arthritis requiring chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy to Adrenal insufficiency (secondary/tertiary, glucocorticoid-induced); individual attribution is not established.

Pharmacological sequence: chronic systemic glucocorticoid therapy prescribed for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis through negative feedback, reducing corticotropin (ACTH) secretion and adrenal cortisol output; secondary (tertiary) adrenal insufficiency may become clinically apparent during tapering or after withdrawal and may persist long after the drug stops. Younes and Younes (PMID 29184808) describe this mechanism directly and note that HPA-axis recovery after cessation is variable and can take 6-12 months. Broersen et al. (PMID 25844620) pooled 74 articles and 3,753 adult corticosteroid users tested for adrenal insufficiency: pooled percentages varied by route from 4.2 percent (nasal) to 52.2 percent (intra-articular) and by disease from 6.8 percent (inhaled-only asthma) to 60.0 percent (hematologic malignancy), with a dose gradient; oral therapy falls within this range. Bowley et al. (PMID 41521083) systematically reviewed only studies using protocolised systemic glucocorticoid regimens and ACTH-stimulation testing, reporting that adrenal insufficiency is a common complication of systemic glucocorticoid therapy with considerable variability; the retrieved abstract excerpt did not expose a pooled estimate, so none is claimed here. These sources establish treatment-mediated causation at the mechanism level while showing that individual risk depends on route, dose, duration, potency, tapering and host factors; no single percentage can be applied to a veteran.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the exact corticosteroid agent(s), route, dose, cumulative duration, taper schedule and stop dates; concurrent topical, inhaled or intra-articular exposure; morning cortisol or ACTH-stimulation results; symptoms such as fatigue, orthostasis, nausea, hyponatremia; and any adrenal-crisis or continued-steroid-dependence events. Document whether insufficiency predated steroid therapy — primary adrenal disease, pituitary pathology, prior pituitary surgery or radiation, opioid effects, checkpoint-inhibitor effects — as competing causes; a pre-existing or independently caused insufficiency changes the theory from § 3.310(a) causation to § 3.310(b) aggravation of a baseline. Recovery testing after withdrawal informs severity and permanence but is not a prerequisite to attributing the insufficiency to treatment.

Legal and rating analysis: 'Medication Side Effect' is treatment-mediated secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a): service-connected rheumatoid arthritis leads through documented corticosteroid exposure to HPA suppression and adrenal insufficiency. If pre-existing adrenal insufficiency was worsened by necessary steroid therapy, analyze aggravation under § 3.310(b) with a documented baseline and attributable decrement beyond the natural course. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the individual's exposure and endocrine chronology plus competing-cause exclusion placing the evidence at least in approximate balance; pooled prevalence does not itself meet that standard. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.119 DC 7911 supplies tiers including corticosteroid therapy required for control (20 percent), one or two crises, or two to four episodes per year; use the actual event counts and treatment requirements. Do not duplicate the same endocrine manifestations under another code (§ 4.14). The rheumatoid arthritis host file is published and currently points only to depressive disorder and GERD; this new incoming route requires host-side review before any landing.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Service-connected rheumatoid arthritis (multi-joint, active or with chronic residuals) to Acquired flatfoot (pes planus with hindfoot valgus) due to rheumatoid arthritis; individual attribution is not established.

Inflammatory-structural sequence: in service-connected rheumatoid arthritis, chronic synovitis erodes the midfoot and hindfoot joints (talonavicular, subtalar and naviculocuneiform) and attacks the tibialis posterior tendon sheath, weakening the dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch; the combination of joint destruction and posterior tibial tendon dysfunction allows progressive valgus collapse of the hindfoot and midfoot — acquired flatfoot. Bouysset et al. (PMID 12022347) obtained weight-bearing radiographs of 308 feet in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and 202 control feet, and found that flat foot increased markedly after three to four years of disease duration, with forefoot deformity progression tracked alongside. Zhao et al. (PMID 39421746), applying bidirectional Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis in European populations, found genetic evidence consistent with rheumatoid arthritis causally contributing to postural deformities including flat foot, and their review of the literature reported flat-foot prevalence of roughly 11.0 to 42.1 percent in rheumatoid arthritis. Mizuki et al. (PMID 41053714) analyzed rheumatoid foot deformity patterns and reported flat foot and hindfoot valgus deformities in the range of 19 to 43 percent, emphasizing that coronal hindfoot alignment drives forefoot deformity. These sources establish rheumatoid arthritis as a recognized cause of acquired flatfoot at population and genetic-instrumental levels; observational and genetic designs cannot determine whether any individual veteran's arch collapse is attributable to the arthritis rather than to an independent cause.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the rheumatoid arthritis by diagnosis and disease duration with inflammatory activity, and characterize the flatfoot with weight-bearing radiographs or clinical measurement of arch height, hindfoot valgus, tenderness and tibialis posterior function; note whether the deformity is flexible or fixed because that determines both mechanism and rating. Congenital or hereditary pes planus, posterior tibial tendon dysfunction unrelated to inflammatory disease, tarsal coalition, Charcot arthropathy (including diabetic Charcot), obesity and mechanical overload, prior trauma or fracture, and tibialis posterior rupture from other causes are competing causes that must be assessed. A temporal sequence in which a previously normal arch collapses after years of active seropositive rheumatoid disease, with radiographic joint erosion and tibialis posterior dysfunction, favors the rheumatoid route; a lifelong flatfoot or a deformity that develops without active inflammatory disease and without joint erosion points to another cause.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected rheumatoid arthritis produces the acquired flatfoot; the theory is causation because a new structural foot disability is generated by the inflammatory disease. If a pre-existing flatfoot or arch insufficiency is asserted to have been worsened, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline (earlier imaging or examination) and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the disease duration and activity, the radiographic erosion pattern, the tibialis posterior findings and the competing-cause analysis to be weighed so that the evidence is at least in approximate balance; prevalence figures and Mendelian randomization do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.71a DC 5276 is the dedicated acquired-flatfoot code, while the primary is rated under DC 5002 during active disease and DC 5003 for chronic residuals; the Note to DCs 5013-5024 is not the operative route for acquired flatfoot. Apply § 4.14 so that the same arch collapse, foot pain or weight-bearing limitation is not rated under both DC 5276 and a DC 5003 residual limitation for the same foot, and apply § 4.25 and the bilateral factor where both feet are separately impaired. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the rheumatoid-arthritis host identity is published and currently points to depressive disorder and GERD, and the flatfoot identity is draft with an outbound association-only suggestion to osteoarthritis and no inbound edges for this inflammatory route.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Service-connected schizophrenia treated with a dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotic to Drug-induced parkinsonism from dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotic exposure; individual attribution is not established.

Pharmacological causal sequence: an antipsychotic prescribed for service-connected schizophrenia can block postsynaptic striatal D2 receptors. In the basal-ganglia motor circuit, D2 blockade disinhibits the indirect-pathway striatal output, increasing downstream inhibitory output to thalamocortical motor systems and producing bradykinesia and rigidity, with tremor or impaired gait in some patients. Shin and Chung (PMID 22523509; full text PMC3325428) describes this circuit and distinguishes postsynaptic blockade from the presynaptic nigrostriatal degeneration typical of idiopathic Parkinson disease. The proximate exposure is the documented medication, not schizophrenia itself. Feldman et al. (PMID 36573102) reviews culprit drugs, differential diagnosis, and management. Ali et al. (PMID 34506552) supplies a systematic review/meta-analysis of observational studies, with pooled antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism prevalence of 20% (95% CI 11-28%). That pooled prevalence quantifies a recognized adverse effect across heterogeneous exposed populations; it is neither a 20% probability that a particular veteran's syndrome is drug-caused nor proof of permanent neurodegeneration.

Required individual evidence: identify the exact antipsychotic, indication, starting date, dose changes, adherence, and concurrent dopamine-blocking medications. Compare dated baseline neurologic findings with the onset of bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor and functional impairment. A compatible onset after initiation or dose escalation and improvement after a clinician-supervised reduction or substitution support attribution, but deliberate rechallenge is not required and medication changes must be coordinated with psychiatry to avoid relapse. Persistence after withdrawal does not exclude a drug contribution; it can reflect prolonged drug effects or unmasking of underlying neurodegenerative disease. Symmetry alone is not diagnostic because drug-induced cases can be asymmetric. Neurologic review should distinguish competing causes, including idiopathic Parkinson disease, vascular parkinsonism, essential tremor, depressive/psychotic psychomotor slowing, tardive dyskinesia, akathisia, and other toxidromes. DAT imaging, when clinically appropriate, may help distinguish presynaptic degeneration from pure postsynaptic blockade but is not a universal required test. Do not relabel tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, or serotonin syndrome as this identity.

Legal theory: 'Medication Side Effect' is the requested packet label. In 38 CFR § 3.310(a) it is a treatment-mediated secondary-causation theory: service-connected schizophrenia → medically documented antipsychotic exposure → drug-induced parkinsonism. It is not a fourth repository nexusClassification enum arm, and no negligence allegation is necessary to describe this secondary-service-connection mechanism. If a pre-existing Parkinson syndrome was instead worsened by necessary antipsychotic treatment, evaluate § 3.310(b) aggravation with a documented baseline and an attributable increase beyond its natural course; do not assert that the drug created the underlying neurodegenerative disease. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the actual exposure chronology, movement-disorder examination, medication response where safely observed, and reasoned consideration of alternatives. No patient-specific probability is asserted here.

Rating and governance controls: schizophrenia uses current DC 9201. Drug-induced parkinsonism has no dedicated code; DC 8004 is identified only as an analogous-rating candidate requiring review of affected function, anatomical localization and symptomatology under §§ 4.20 and 4.27. Do not apply its minimum rating automatically, equate this syndrome with idiopathic Parkinson disease, or duplicate the same manifestations under § 4.14. The repository's batch-95 deferral and ME-29 held-evidence adjudication remain active. This newly located independent systematic-review anchor is presented for human reassessment, not an automatic lifting of that hold; reserved PMIDs 30695288 and 34652577 are not reused in this proposal.

suggestions.rationale:
Staging-only research proposal, not a signed medical opinion or publication approval. No patient records were supplied. No individual probability is asserted here. Population associations and mechanism plausibility do not establish an individual nexus.

Original proposal mechanism (preserved verbatim):
Pharmacological causal sequence: an antipsychotic prescribed for service-connected schizophrenia can block postsynaptic striatal D2 receptors. In the basal-ganglia motor circuit, D2 blockade disinhibits the indirect-pathway striatal output, increasing downstream inhibitory output to thalamocortical motor systems and producing bradykinesia and rigidity, with tremor or impaired gait in some patients. Shin and Chung (PMID 22523509; full text PMC3325428) describes this circuit and distinguishes postsynaptic blockade from the presynaptic nigrostriatal degeneration typical of idiopathic Parkinson disease. The proximate exposure is the documented medication, not schizophrenia itself. Feldman et al. (PMID 36573102) reviews culprit drugs, differential diagnosis, and management. Ali et al. (PMID 34506552) supplies a systematic review/meta-analysis of observational studies, with pooled antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism prevalence of 20% (95% CI 11-28%). That pooled prevalence quantifies a recognized adverse effect across heterogeneous exposed populations; it is neither a 20% probability that a particular veteran's syndrome is drug-caused nor proof of permanent neurodegeneration.

Required individual evidence: identify the exact antipsychotic, indication, starting date, dose changes, adherence, and concurrent dopamine-blocking medications. Compare dated baseline neurologic findings with the onset of bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor and functional impairment. A compatible onset after initiation or dose escalation and improvement after a clinician-supervised reduction or substitution support attribution, but deliberate rechallenge is not required and medication changes must be coordinated with psychiatry to avoid relapse. Persistence after withdrawal does not exclude a drug contribution; it can reflect prolonged drug effects or unmasking of underlying neurodegenerative disease. Symmetry alone is not diagnostic because drug-induced cases can be asymmetric. Neurologic review should distinguish competing causes, including idiopathic Parkinson disease, vascular parkinsonism, essential tremor, depressive/psychotic psychomotor slowing, tardive dyskinesia, akathisia, and other toxidromes. DAT imaging, when clinically appropriate, may help distinguish presynaptic degeneration from pure postsynaptic blockade but is not a universal required test. Do not relabel tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, or serotonin syndrome as this identity.

Legal theory: 'Medication Side Effect' is the requested packet label. In 38 CFR § 3.310(a) it is a treatment-mediated secondary-causation theory: service-connected schizophrenia → medically documented antipsychotic exposure → drug-induced parkinsonism. It is not a fourth repository nexusClassification enum arm, and no negligence allegation is necessary to describe this secondary-service-connection mechanism. If a pre-existing Parkinson syndrome was instead worsened by necessary antipsychotic treatment, evaluate § 3.310(b) aggravation with a documented baseline and an attributable increase beyond its natural course; do not assert that the drug created the underlying neurodegenerative disease. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the actual exposure chronology, movement-disorder examination, medication response where safely observed, and reasoned consideration of alternatives. No patient-specific probability is asserted here.

Rating and governance controls: schizophrenia uses current DC 9201. Drug-induced parkinsonism has no dedicated code; DC 8004 is identified only as an analogous-rating candidate requiring review of affected function, anatomical localization and symptomatology under §§ 4.20 and 4.27. nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Service-connected systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), with documented cutaneous or visceral involvement to Raynaud's syndrome (secondary Raynaud's phenomenon with digital vasospasm, and its digital ulcer and auto-amputation sequelae) in a veteran with service-connected systemic sclerosis; individual attribution is not established.

Microvascular and fibrotic vascular sequence: in service-connected systemic sclerosis, endothelial injury with intimal proliferation and progressive obliterative vasculopathy narrows the digital arteries and arterioles, while platelet activation, increased endothelin-1 and reduced nitric oxide and prostacyclin signaling shift the digital vascular bed toward vasoconstriction and impaired vasodilation. The consequence is an exaggerated, reversible digital vasospasm in response to cold or emotional stress — Raynaud's phenomenon — which in systemic sclerosis is not a benign primary disorder but a marker and driver of progressive digital ischemia; when the vasospasm and fixed structural narrowing coexist, persistent hypoperfusion produces digital pitting scars, ischemic ulcers, and auto-amputation of fingertips. Hughes et al. (PMID 32099191) state that Raynaud phenomenon occurs in virtually all patients with systemic sclerosis and is often the earliest clinical manifestation, and that it is caused by impaired digital perfusion requiring careful assessment. Sunderkötter and Riemekasten (PMID 16987831) describe Raynaud's phenomenon in systemic sclerosis as an initial event in the pathophysiological cascade leading to sclerosis, characterized by recurrent reversible spasms of small arterioles and digital arteries triggered by cold and emotional stress and producing the characteristic sudden pallor of the digits. Maciejewska et al. (PMID 35566614) review Raynaud's phenomenon with a focus on systemic sclerosis and state that systemic sclerosis is one of the most frequent causes of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon and that its appearance may occur long before other signs and symptoms, emphasizing the treatment distinction between primary and secondary forms. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected systemic sclerosis is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated vascular condition, secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, with its own diagnostic code at DC 7117 rather than being folded into the skin or musculoskeletal evaluation of the scleroderma itself. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; an aggravation theory would be required only where the record shows pre-existing primary Raynaud's disease (DC 7124) or cold-injury-related vasospasm and the claim is that the systemic sclerosis measurably worsened a baseline vasospastic disorder, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the primary disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require documented systemic sclerosis with American College of Rheumatology or EULAR classification features (for example, sclerodactyly, specific autoantibodies, nailfold capillary abnormalities, or internal-organ involvement), a clinical description of characteristic attacks meeting the DC 7117 note definition — sequential digital color change lasting minutes to hours, precipitated by cold or emotional stress — and a temporal relationship in which the vasospastic attacks begin with or after disease onset. Where digital ulcers or auto-amputation are asserted for the 60 or 100 percent tiers, the ulcer history and imaging or photographic documentation must be of record. Only then can an examiner state that the Raynaud's syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected systemic sclerosis — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include primary Raynaud's disease (which is the schedule's separate DC 7124 entity), cold-injury residuals under DC 7122 (whose note directs separate evaluation of Raynaud's syndrome unless those findings already support an evaluation there), cigarette smoking and other vasoconstrictor exposure, beta-blocker, ergotamine, or stimulant medication, hypothyroidism, carpal tunnel syndrome and thoracic outlet syndrome, vibration-tool exposure, cryoglobulinemia, and other connective tissue diseases such as mixed connective tissue disease or systemic lupus erythematosus, which are distinct service-connected or non-service-connected identities and must not be merged with systemic sclerosis. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: DC 7117 evaluations are for Raynaud's syndrome as a whole, so the same digital attacks, ulcers, or amputations may not be compensated a second time under the cold-injury code or as residuals of the scleroderma skin evaluation, and separate amputation ratings follow only the amputation rule and the schedule's own provisions.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Service-connected testicular germ-cell malignancy treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy to Sensorineural hearing loss associated with cisplatin ototoxicity; individual attribution is not established.

Treatment-mediated sequence: service-connected testicular cancer → documented cisplatin exposure → cochlear injury → sensorineural hearing loss. Paken et al. (PMID 28115933; PMC5223030) describes reactive-oxygen-species generation, depletion of antioxidant defenses and apoptotic injury, most prominently involving outer hair cells in the basal cochlear turn; supporting cells, stria vascularis and spiral-ganglion structures can also be affected. Basal-turn vulnerability explains why high-frequency thresholds may deteriorate first, with lower-frequency involvement as injury increases. These molecular pathways draw partly on experimental research and are not biomarkers proving an individual nexus. The typical pattern is bilateral high-frequency sensorineural impairment, often with tinnitus, but perfect symmetry is not required and an atypical pattern requires a careful differential. This is a treatment effect, not a claim that the testicular tumor directly invades the cochlea.

Human evidence: Frisina et al. (PMID 27354478) studied 488 male germ-cell-tumor survivors and found a dose-response relationship: each additional 100 mg/m² of cumulative cisplatin was associated with 3.2 dB worse age-adjusted thresholds across 4-12 kHz. This survivor analysis does not supply a pretreatment audiogram for each participant and its ASHA-defined severity is not a VA rating. Haugnes et al. (PMID 29384420) provides longitudinal pretreatment/follow-up data in 46 treated testicular-cancer survivors with 46 untreated matched survivors. Age and dose mattered; at 8 kHz each additional 100 mg of cumulative dose was associated with 3.6 dB deterioration as reported in that abstract. Do not replace its dose unit with mg/m². The ASHA-defined follow-up case/control difference was nonsignificant (70% versus 65%, P=.66), while a four-frequency definition differed (13% versus 2.2%, P=.049). This definitional counterweight prevents exaggerating attributable clinical disability.

Individual evidence and competing causes: obtain cancer treatment records, cumulative cisplatin dose and dates, baseline and serial air/bone-conduction audiograms, speech results, tympanometry, tinnitus history and functional reports. Extended-frequency monitoring can detect early ototoxic change but does not replace conventional VA testing. Consider pre-existing military/occupational/recreational noise exposure, presbycusis, familial loss, middle-ear disease, vestibular schwannoma or another asymmetric lesion, renal impairment, and other ototoxic drugs. Renal impairment may modify exposure risk but does not independently prove attribution. Serial threshold changes during or after treatment and a compatible cochlear pattern support the chain; absence of baseline testing creates uncertainty, not an automatic positive or negative opinion.

Legal and rating analysis: the packet's 'Medication Side Effect' label represents § 3.310(a) treatment-mediated causation when service-connected cancer treatment produces the impairment. If hearing loss predated chemotherapy, separately address § 3.310(b) aggravation, comparing the qualifying baseline with current severity and separating an attributable treatment increment from natural age/noise-related progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs veteran-specific chronology, audiometric change and a reasoned competing-cause assessment placing evidence at least in approximate balance; general ototoxicity or cohort prevalence alone is insufficient. No individual probability is asserted here. § 3.385 requires a threshold of at least 40 dB at any of 500/1000/2000/3000/4000 Hz, at least 26 dB at three of those frequencies, or Maryland CNC recognition below 94%. § 4.85 requires state-licensed audiology, appropriate puretone and Maryland CNC testing without hearing aids, and a 1000/2000/3000/4000-Hz average, subject to its stated exceptions. A change confined to 8-12 kHz can be medically important without meeting VA disability or compensable-rating criteria. (PMID 27354478) studied 488 male germ-cell-tumor survivors and found a dose-response relationship: each additional 100 mg/m² of cumulative cisplatin was associated with 3.2 dB worse age-adjusted thresholds across 4-12 kHz. causalMechanism.primaryVector: Persistent tinnitus can aggravate an existing migraine diathesis through converging neurophysiological and behavioral mechanisms. Tinnitus is not a passive percept: chronic cochlear injury and deafferentation trigger maladaptive central plasticity, increased central auditory gain, and thalamocortical dysrhythmia, with limbic and salience-network modulation that attaches threat and distress to the sound; stress and sleep disruption further entrench the maladaptive state. In a brain already predisposed to migraine — a disorder of multisensory sensitization — this persistent auditory load lowers attack threshold through central sensitization, cortical hyperexcitability, and overlapping neurochemical pathways (glutamatergic excitotoxicity, neuropeptide signaling, and innate immune activation), while the distress, hypervigilance, and sleep fragmentation that accompany bothersome tinnitus amplify trigeminovascular activation and reduce habituation. The clinical literature documents the intersection: a systematic review of six studies (26,166 participants) found most studies demonstrating an association between migraine and tinnitus, with high odds and hazard ratios for tinnitus in migraine populations and migraine present in 10.1% and 22.5% of tinnitus patients in two studies; a 2026 review reports that 15-49% of migraine patients have comorbid auditory symptoms including tinnitus and that nearly two-thirds show auditory electrophysiological abnormalities; and the current authoritative tinnitus review identifies migraine, anxiety, depression, and insomnia as frequent comorbidities and describes the central-gain and thalamocortical-dysrhythmia mechanisms that plausibly drive bidirectional symptom amplification. Because most of the located evidence is cross-sectional or directionally weighted toward migraine as the exposure (migraine-to-tinnitus), this mapping is framed as aggravation under 38 CFR § 3.310(b), not as de novo causation: service connection is warranted only for the increase in migraine frequency, severity, or prostration proximately attributable to service-connected tinnitus, measured against a baseline established by medical evidence created before the aggravation or the earliest evidence between onset and current severity. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the pre-tinnitus migraine baseline (attack frequency, duration, and disability before tinnitus onset), the timing and severity of the tinnitus and its associated distress and sleep disruption, the subsequent change in migraine pattern, and effective audiologic and neurologic evaluation; exclude medication-overuse headache, new-onset primary headache, structural or vascular causes, and independent progression of the underlying migraine disorder. Where no pre-existing migraine is documented, a causation theory under § 3.310(a) may be advanced, but it requires temporal precedence of the tinnitus and an individualized opinion because the located population evidence does not establish the tinnitus-to-migraine direction.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Traumatic brain injury (service-connected), with residuals to Post-traumatic headache (persistent, migraine or tension-type phenotype); individual attribution is not established.

Post-traumatic headache (PTH) is a secondary headache disorder attributable to the direct and downstream effects of traumatic brain injury (TBI) on nociceptive and trigeminovascular systems. The injury cascade begins with mechanical loading of cranial and cervical structures at impact, producing axonal shearing, glial activation, and neuroinflammation in pain-modulating networks (trigeminocervical complex, thalamus, periaqueductal gray, somatosensory cortex), together with diminished descending pain inhibition and central sensitization. These changes lower the threshold for activation of the trigeminovascular system, where calcitonin gene-related peptide release, meningeal nociceptor sensitization, cortical spreading depression susceptibility, and autonomic dysregulation generate migraine-like attacks; a parallel myofascial and cervicogenic contribution arises from injury to cervical muscles and joints, producing tension-type presentations. Comorbid sleep disruption, vestibular dysfunction, and post-traumatic stress are amplifying rather than initiating factors, and medication-overuse headache can secondarily maintain the pattern. The clinical epidemiology is robust: pooled prevalence of headache after TBI is 49.3% (95% CI 44.7-53.9) across observational studies, and persistent post-traumatic headache in adult civilians is 47.1% (95% CI 34.6-59.8) with similar estimates at 3, 6, 12, and 36-plus months; in a prospective multi-center cohort, 71% of patients reported headache during the first year after injury and more than 41% still reported headache at 3, 6, and 12 months, with incidence unrelated to TBI severity (p = 0.67) but significantly related to pre-injury headache history (p < 0.001) and female sex (p < 0.01). Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a persistent headache disorder developing after a service-connected TBI is a direct-causation secondary claim, and PTH is not among the conditions listed in § 3.310(d)(1), so the nexus rests on an individual medical opinion rather than a regulatory presumption. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI (with severity at the time of injury), the headache chronology relative to the injury (onset within days to weeks and persistence beyond three months), semiology consistent with the International Classification of Headache Disorders criteria for headache attributed to traumatic injury to the head, and treatment response; exclude or address primary migraine or tension-type headache predating the injury, medication-overuse headache, cervicogenic headache, and secondary causes (vascular, intracranial pressure, infection). If a pre-existing headache disorder is documented, § 3.310(b) permits service connection only for the attributable aggravation, measured against an established baseline rather than the natural progression of the pre-existing disorder.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Traumatic brain injury (service-connected), with residuals to Peripheral vestibular dysfunction (including traumatic benign paroxysmal positional vertigo); individual attribution is not established.

Traumatic brain injury disrupts the peripheral vestibular system through mechanical and vascular injury. Impact forces transmitted to the temporal bone and labyrinth produce labyrinthine concussion with damage to the membranous labyrinth and sensory epithelia; acceleration-deceleration of the head shears the otolithic membrane and dislodges otoconia from the utricle, which migrate into a semicircular canal (most often the posterior canal) and cause positionally triggered endolymph flow — the canalithiasis mechanism of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV). Additional contributions include direct injury to the vestibular nerve, hemorrhage or ischemia of the labyrinth and brainstem vestibular nuclei, and central vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal dysfunction that may coexist with the peripheral lesion; the clinical result is vertigo and positional dizziness, imbalance, gait instability, oscillopsia, nausea, and visual-vestibular intolerance. Severity and timing track trauma severity: in a prospective series of 117 patients with minimal, mild, or moderate head trauma examined with Dix-Hallpike and supine roll testing, 21% developed traumatic BPPV within three months (12%, 24%, and 40% across minimal, mild, and moderate trauma, respectively; p = 0.018), with nearly all onsets in the first four weeks; in a systematic review of 23 studies of non-blast TBI, BPPV was the most frequently identified peripheral vestibular deficit, diagnosed in 39.7% of 239 participants across six studies, though most data were retrospective and from tertiary centers, and a 2025 systematic review of 59 studies documents the spectrum of vestibular dysfunction after mild TBI, including dizziness, imbalance, vertigo, vestibulo-ocular dysfunction, and nystagmus, and the role of vestibular rehabilitation. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a peripheral vestibular disorder developing after a service-connected TBI is a direct-causation secondary claim; vestibular dysfunction is not among the conditions listed in § 3.310(d)(1), so an individual medical opinion is required. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI, the onset and pattern of positional vertigo or imbalance relative to the injury, and objective vestibular findings (positive Dix-Hallpike or supine roll maneuver with characteristic nystagmus for BPPV; videonystagmography, video head impulse, caloric, or vestibular-evoked myogenic potential testing for non-positional deficits), and address competing causes — pre-existing or idiopathic BPPV (common in the general population, so temporal proximity to trauma is essential), vestibular migraine, Meniere's disease, medication ototoxicity, and central or cerebellar causes. Where a pre-existing vestibular disorder is documented, § 3.310(b) permits service connection only for the attributable aggravation over the established baseline.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Traumatic brain injury (moderate or severe, service-connected), with residuals to Hypopituitarism (anterior pituitary hormone deficiency following traumatic brain injury); individual attribution is not established.

Traumatic brain injury causes hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction through several converging mechanisms. Direct mechanical forces can fracture the skull base and sella, shear the pituitary stalk, and injure the median eminence, while rotational acceleration damages the fine hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal vasculature and the pituitary itself. Subsequent edema, hemorrhage, and hypoxic-ischemic injury (from apnea, hypotension, or raised intracranial pressure) further compromise the hypothalamic neurons and pituitary secretory cells that regulate the axes. The result is deficient synthesis or release of one or more anterior pituitary hormones: growth hormone (most commonly), gonadotropins leading to hypogonadism, thyrotropin leading to central hypothyroidism, corticotropin leading to secondary adrenal insufficiency, and less commonly antidiuretic hormone deficiency. Early post-injury abnormalities may be transient, but a substantial proportion of patients develop persistent deficits that are detectable at 12 months or later, and untreated deficiency produces fatigue, impaired quality of life, adverse metabolic profiles, and impaired recovery. The evidence base is quantitative and consistent: a systematic review pooling 19 studies of 1,137 patients found chronic-phase hypopituitarism in 27.5% (95% CI 22.8-28.9) after TBI, with higher prevalence after severe TBI; a meta-analysis of 29 studies and 2,756 participants found at least one anterior pituitary hormone dysfunction in 32% (95% CI 25-38) at 12 months or more (34% in high-quality studies); and a 2024 meta-analysis of 52 studies and 7,367 participants found any pituitary axis dysfunction in 33% (95% CI 28-37), with growth hormone deficiency 18%, gonadal deficiency 16%, ACTH deficiency 10%, and TSH deficiency 6%, and multiple affected axes in 7%. Legally, 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1)(v) provides that diseases of hormone deficiency that result from hypothalamo-pituitary changes are presumed to be the proximate result of a service-connected TBI when they manifest within 12 months of moderate or severe TBI; where that presumption does not apply (mild TBI, or manifestation outside 12 months), § 3.310(d)(2) directs decision under generally applicable principles, i.e., a § 3.310(a) causation opinion. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria (loss of consciousness, alteration of consciousness, post-traumatic amnesia, Glasgow Coma Scale, imaging), the date of manifestation of the hormone deficiency relative to the injury, and endocrinologic testing of the affected axes (morning cortisol with stimulation testing where indicated, IGF-1, LH/FSH with testosterone or estradiol, TSH with free T4, prolactin, and sodium/osmolality for diabetes insipidus), and exclude competing causes — pituitary adenoma or other sellar mass, cranial radiotherapy, hypophysitis, Sheehan's syndrome, hemochromatosis, infiltrative disease, and drug effects.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Traumatic brain injury (moderate or severe, service-connected), with residuals to Seizure disorder (post-traumatic epilepsy, unprovoked seizures); individual attribution is not established.

Traumatic brain injury produces epilepsy through a well-characterized epileptogenic cascade. Focal cortical contusion, subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhage, and shearing of white-matter tracts create a structural lesion with hemosiderin deposition, blood-brain-barrier disruption, and reactive gliosis; injured neurons and glia release glutamate and inflammatory mediators that produce excitotoxic injury, while loss of inhibitory interneurons and aberrant axonal sprouting (mossy fiber reorganization) establish a hyperexcitable network capable of spontaneous seizure generation. The latent period between injury and the first unprovoked seizure reflects this progressive epileptogenesis, and lesional features visible on imaging (cortical contusion, subdural hematoma) are among the most consistently reported risk factors. The epidemiological evidence is strong and severity-dependent: a population-based cohort of 4,541 patients with TBI (Olmsted County, 1935-1984) found an overall standardized incidence ratio of 3.1 (95% CI 2.5-3.8), with SIR 1.5 after mild injury (no increase beyond five years), 2.9 after moderate injury, and 17.0 after severe injury; a Danish population-based cohort of 1,605,216 people found relative risks of 2.22 (95% CI 2.07-2.38) after mild injury, 7.40 (6.16-8.89) after severe injury, and 2.17 (1.73-2.71) after skull fracture, with risk still elevated more than 10 years later (severe injury RR 4.29, 95% CI 2.04-9.00) and especially high in those injured after age 15 (severe injury RR 12.24, 95% CI 8.52-17.57); and a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies (242,803 patients) found a pooled post-traumatic seizure incidence of 7.2% (95% CI 5.4-9.3), with severe TBI, subdural hematoma, cortical contusions, and older age the most consistently reported risk factors in individual studies. Legally, 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1)(ii) provides that unprovoked seizures following moderate or severe TBI are held to be the proximate result of the service-connected TBI absent clear evidence to the contrary; where the injury was mild or the claim falls outside the presumption, § 3.310(d)(2) routes the claim to generally applicable principles and a § 3.310(a) opinion. nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Traumatic brain injury (moderate or severe, service-connected), with residuals to Dementia / major neurocognitive disorder (TBI-associated); individual attribution is not established.

Traumatic brain injury increases the long-term risk of dementia through injury-driven neurodegenerative and vascular mechanisms. Focal contusions, diffuse axonal injury, and microhemorrhages initiate persistent neuroinflammation (microglial and astrocytic activation), blood-brain-barrier disruption, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired protein clearance, promoting accumulation of amyloid-beta and hyperphosphorylated tau; these proteinopathies, together with synaptic loss and reduced cognitive reserve, are the leading hypotheses linking TBI to Alzheimer-type and related dementias. Injury to small vessels and repeated episodes of impaired perfusion contribute an additional vascular burden. Several features support a causal rather than coincidental relationship: risk is dose-dependent (increasing with the number and severity of injuries), persists over decades, and is present when TBI is compared both with uninjured people and with people who sustained non-head trauma. Quantitatively, a Danish nationwide cohort of 2,794,852 people (27.6 million person-years; 132,093 with at least one TBI) found a fully adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause dementia of 1.24 (95% CI 1.21-1.27) and for Alzheimer's disease 1.16 (1.12-1.22), with the highest risk in the first six months after injury (HR 4.06, 3.79-4.34) and a graded increase with the number of TBIs (HR 1.22 after one, rising to 2.83 after five or more); a meta-analysis of 32 studies found a pooled risk ratio of 1.66 (95% CI 1.42-1.93) for dementia after TBI, with the population attributable risk among U.S. veterans twice that of the general population; and a veteran-specific meta-analysis of 13 cohorts (more than 7.1 million observations) found all-cause dementia HR 1.95 (95% CI 1.55-2.45) and vascular dementia HR 2.02 (1.46-2.80), with higher risk after severe or penetrating injury (HR 3.35) than after moderate (2.82) or mild (1.91) injury, while the association with Alzheimer's disease alone was not statistically significant (HR 1.30, 0.88-1.91). Legally, 38 CFR § 3.310(d)(1)(iii) provides that presenile dementia of the Alzheimer type, frontotemporal dementia, and dementia with Lewy bodies are held to be the proximate result of a service-connected TBI if they manifest within 15 years following moderate or severe TBI; the presumption is diagnosis- and timing-specific, and dementias outside that list (including vascular dementia) are decided under § 3.310(d)(2) on generally applicable principles with a § 3.310(a) opinion. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity under § 3.310(d)(3), the dementia phenotype with formal neurocognitive testing and the date of manifestation relative to the injury, and the neurologic, psychiatric, and laboratory workup; exclude competing causes — Alzheimer's disease occurring independently of trauma, vascular dementia from hypertension or stroke, Parkinson's disease and Lewy body disease occurring independently, alcohol-related cognitive impairment, medication effects, depression with cognitive symptoms, thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, and normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Where cognitive decline predates the injury or arises from another established cause, only attributable aggravation can be service-connected under § 3.310(b).

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Traumatic brain injury (service-connected), with residuals to Insomnia disorder (chronic, post-traumatic); individual attribution is not established.

Traumatic brain injury produces chronic insomnia through structural and functional injury to the sleep-wake regulatory system rather than through pain or psychological factors alone. The ascending arousal system (brainstem cholinergic and monoaminergic nuclei), the hypothalamic sleep-wake switch including orexin/hypocretin neurons, the suprachiasmatic nucleus and its light-entrainment input, and the thalamocortical circuits that generate sleep spindles are all vulnerable to shearing, contusion, and hypoxic-ischemic injury; diffuse axonal injury and neuroinflammation (microglial activation with cytokine release, including interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor) further disturb sleep homeostasis and circadian timing. Clinically this produces sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance insomnia, fragmentation, and non-restorative sleep, often with excessive daytime sleepiness, and the disturbance can persist for years after the injury and impede rehabilitation. The epidemiologic evidence is substantial: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies (19 meta-analyzed, n = 95,195) found pooled prevalence of post-mild-TBI insomnia disorder of 27.0% (95% CI 6.49-54.68) and insomnia symptoms of 71.7% (95% CI 60.31-81.85), significantly higher than general-population estimates, though heterogeneity was high; a second, larger synthesis of 69 studies found adults with prior mild TBI reported worse subjective sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index elevations) at every recovery phase from under a week to one year and beyond, while objective sleep-stage differences were less robust after bias adjustment; and a mechanistic review documents the neural-network, neuroendocrine, sleep-wake-regulator, and immune-inflammatory pathways implicated in post-TBI sleep-wake disturbance. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a chronic insomnia disorder developing after a service-connected TBI is a direct-causation secondary claim; insomnia is not among the conditions listed in § 3.310(d)(1), so an individual medical opinion is required. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria, the sleep history with onset relative to the injury and persistence over time (sleep diary, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index or insomnia severity measures, and polysomnography where indicated), and the treatment history; exclude or account for competing causes — obstructive and central sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements, circadian rhythm disorders, pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and depression, substance and medication effects (including stimulants and sedatives), and primary insomnia predating the injury. Where pre-existing insomnia is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation, and where insomnia is a symptom of an already service-connected mental disorder, § 4.14 prohibits duplicate evaluation.

Clinically this produces sleep-onset and sleep-maintenance insomnia, fragmentation, and non-restorative sleep, often with excessive daytime sleepiness, and the disturbance can persist for years after the injury and impede rehabilitation. The epidemiologic evidence is substantial: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies (19 meta-analyzed, n = 95,195) found pooled prevalence of post-mild-TBI insomnia disorder of 27.0% (95% CI 6.49-54.68) and insomnia symptoms of 71.7% (95% CI 60.31-81.85), significantly higher than general-population estimates, though heterogeneity was high; a second, larger synthesis of 69 studies found adults with prior mild TBI reported worse subjective sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index elevations) at every recovery phase from under a week to one year and beyond, while objective sleep-stage differences were less robust after bias adjustment; and a mechanistic review documents the neural-network, neuroendocrine, sleep-wake-regulator, and immune-inflammatory pathways implicated in post-TBI sleep-wake disturbance. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a chronic insomnia disorder developing after a service-connected TBI is a direct-causation secondary claim; insomnia is not among the conditions listed in § 3.310(d)(1), so an individual medical opinion is required. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the TBI and its severity using the § 3.310(d)(3) criteria, the sleep history with onset relative to the injury and persistence over time (sleep diary, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index or insomnia severity measures, and polysomnography where indicated), and the treatment history; exclude or account for competing causes — obstructive and central sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movements, circadian rhythm disorders, pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety and depression, substance and medication effects (including stimulants and sedatives), and primary insomnia predating the injury. Where pre-existing insomnia is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation, and where insomnia is a symptom of an already service-connected mental disorder, § 4.14 prohibits duplicate evaluation.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Service-connected residual deficits of traumatic brain injury (TBI) to Heterotopic ossification (neurogenic) complicating traumatic brain injury; individual attribution is not established.

Neurogenic sequence: severe traumatic brain injury is associated with neurogenic heterotopic ossification (NHO), aberrant lamellar bone forming in periarticular soft tissues — characteristically around the hips, elbows and shoulders — causing pain and loss of joint motion. Sullivan et al. (PMID 23610702) review that NHO affects approximately one in five patients sustaining spinal cord injury or traumatic brain injury, and describe pathophysiology coupling basic bone-formation mechanisms with systemic circulating humoral factors and likely neurological influences; clinical sequelae include pressure injuries, urinary tract infection and pneumonia, making early recognition important. Simonsen et al. (PMID 17572418) studied 114 consecutive adults with very severe TBI (post-traumatic amnesia at least 28 days) and found clinically significant HO in 7.9 percent, noting literature incidence from 11 to 73.3 percent depending on ascertainment. Aubut et al. (PMID 21447915) systematically reviewed 26 treatment studies (12 TBI, 14 SCI) and found the TBI evidence base dominated by surgical case series with limited randomized evidence. Collectively these sources establish TBI as a recognized cause of heterotopic ossification while showing that incidence estimates are highly method-dependent and the causal mechanism is incompletely understood. HO frequently coexists with long-bone fractures and spasticity; the TBI-related contribution must be separated from fracture callus and immobilization effects.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the TBI history and severity, timing relative to HO onset, joint examination with range-of-motion loss, serial radiographs/CT or bone scan, alkaline phosphatase and laboratory context, and operative pathology when resected. The differential includes fracture callus or nonunion, post-traumatic arthritis, infection, deep venous thrombosis and tumor; competing causes also include heterotopic bone arising from associated long-bone trauma or burns rather than the brain injury. HO is not caused by TBI in isolation: immobilization, spasticity and associated fractures modify risk, and a veteran with ossification at a fracture site may have the fracture as a co-cause. Early diagnosis before joint ankylosis is clinically important.

Legal and rating analysis: direct secondary causation under § 3.310(a) applies when the service-connected TBI and its clinical course produce the heterotopic ossification. If a pre-existing ossification or joint condition was worsened, analyze § 3.310(b) aggravation with qualifying baseline imaging/function and an attributable increase beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the veteran-specific TBI-to-HO chronology, location concordance with typical periarticular distributions, and competing-cause assessment; population incidence ranges cannot substitute for that balancing. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.71a DC 5023 is a dedicated code for heterotopic ossification, evaluated on limitation of motion under the Note to DCs 5013-5024. The TBI primary is rated under § 4.124a DC 8045; do not use the same limitation of motion to support both the DC 8045 physical-residual evaluation and the DC 5023 rating (§ 4.14). The heterotopic-ossification identity's existing governance authors only an association-only outgoing edge to peripheral neuropathy; this new incoming route from TBI residuals should be reviewed against that conservative posture.

nexusClaim.etiologicalTrigger:
Proposed route from Service-connected residuals of traumatic brain injury, with a documented closed-head or blast injury and persistent physical residuals including balance or vestibular dysfunction to Meniere's disease (secondary endolymphatic hydrops) following service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals; individual attribution is not established.

Post-traumatic inner-ear fluid-homeostasis sequence: a blow to the head or a blast overpressure event delivers shearing and hydraulic force to the labyrinth, to the temporal bone, and to the endolymphatic sac and duct. Mechanical disruption of the membranous labyrinth allows potassium-rich endolymph to contaminate perilymph, depolarizing hair cells and producing episodic vertigo; injury or obstruction of the endolymphatic duct and sac impairs longitudinal flow and resorption of endolymph, so endolymphatic volume rises and secondary endolymphatic hydrops develops with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and recurrent vertigo — the clinical profile of Meniere's disease. Ferster et al. (PMID 28306649) review secondary endolymphatic hydrops and identify it as a pathologic finding of the inner ear producing episodic vertigo and intermittent hearing loss, with post-mortem temporal-bone histopathology demonstrating hydrops in a post-traumatic case. Chung et al. (PMID 24782951) report a case of post-traumatic Meniere's disease in which the patient developed tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and recurrent vertigo, with symptom improvement only after endolymphatic sac decompression surgery, documenting a trauma-triggered hydrops that behaved as Meniere's disease. DiBiase and Arriaga (PMID 9386247) state that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity based on clinical observation and histopathologic study, and that the traumatic insult may be a blow to the head or a temporal bone fracture, while they also record that many cases of Meniere's disease have no identifiable etiologic agent — an important limitation that the individual nexus opinion must confront rather than ignore. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals are asserted to have caused a distinct inner-ear disease rated separately under DC 6205. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record shows idiopathic Meniere's disease or pre-existing vestibular disease before the head injury and the claim is that the trauma measurably worsened a baseline disorder, in which case the trauma-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the corresponding individual analysis require documentation that the head injury preceded the onset of the vertiginous and fluctuating hearing symptoms, that vestibular and audiologic testing supports endolymphatic hydrops (for example, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with episodic vertigo), and that the examiner can state that the Meniere's disease is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected traumatic brain injury — an opinion that requires a documented temporal sequence, an accounting for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include idiopathic Meniere's disease without any traumatic trigger, viral labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, otosclerosis, autoimmune inner ear disease, syphilis, noise-induced cochlear injury, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, migraine-associated vertigo, and acoustic trauma, together with a positive family history of Meniere's disease; the discrimination is clinically demanding because most head injuries do not cause hydrops and because Meniere's disease is itself usually idiopathic. No individual probability is asserted here. Two rating cautions apply. First, DC 8045 itself forbids rating the same manifestation twice: vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss routed to DC 6205 may not simultaneously be used in the traumatic-brain-injury subjective-symptoms facet, consistent with § 4.14 non-pyramiding. Second, the note to DC 6205 bars combining an evaluation under DC 6205 with separate evaluations of hearing impairment, tinnitus, or vertigo, so only one coherent rating construct may be used.
