Original proposal mechanism (preserved verbatim):
Post-traumatic inner-ear fluid-homeostasis sequence: a blow to the head or a blast overpressure event delivers shearing and hydraulic force to the labyrinth, to the temporal bone, and to the endolymphatic sac and duct. Mechanical disruption of the membranous labyrinth allows potassium-rich endolymph to contaminate perilymph, depolarizing hair cells and producing episodic vertigo; injury or obstruction of the endolymphatic duct and sac impairs longitudinal flow and resorption of endolymph, so endolymphatic volume rises and secondary endolymphatic hydrops develops with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and recurrent vertigo — the clinical profile of Meniere's disease. Ferster et al. (PMID 28306649) review secondary endolymphatic hydrops and identify it as a pathologic finding of the inner ear producing episodic vertigo and intermittent hearing loss, with post-mortem temporal-bone histopathology demonstrating hydrops in a post-traumatic case. Chung et al. (PMID 24782951) report a case of post-traumatic Meniere's disease in which the patient developed tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and recurrent vertigo, with symptom improvement only after endolymphatic sac decompression surgery, documenting a trauma-triggered hydrops that behaved as Meniere's disease. DiBiase and Arriaga (PMID 9386247) state that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity based on clinical observation and histopathologic study, and that the traumatic insult may be a blow to the head or a temporal bone fracture, while they also record that many cases of Meniere's disease have no identifiable etiologic agent — an important limitation that the individual nexus opinion must confront rather than ignore. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory, in which the service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals are asserted to have caused a distinct inner-ear disease rated separately under DC 6205. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record shows idiopathic Meniere's disease or pre-existing vestibular disease before the head injury and the claim is that the trauma measurably worsened a baseline disorder, in which case the trauma-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the corresponding individual analysis require documentation that the head injury preceded the onset of the vertiginous and fluctuating hearing symptoms, that vestibular and audiologic testing supports endolymphatic hydrops (for example, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with episodic vertigo), and that the examiner can state that the Meniere's disease is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected traumatic brain injury — an opinion that requires a documented temporal sequence, an accounting for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include idiopathic Meniere's disease without any traumatic trigger, viral labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, otosclerosis, autoimmune inner ear disease, syphilis, noise-induced cochlear injury, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, migraine-associated vertigo, and acoustic trauma, together with a positive family history of Meniere's disease; the discrimination is clinically demanding because most head injuries do not cause hydrops and because Meniere's disease is itself usually idiopathic. No individual probability is asserted here. Two rating cautions apply. First, DC 8045 itself forbids rating the same manifestation twice: vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss routed to DC 6205 may not simultaneously be used in the traumatic-brain-injury subjective-symptoms facet, consistent with § 4.14 non-pyramiding. Second, the note to DC 6205 bars combining an evaluation under DC 6205 with separate evaluations of hearing impairment, tinnitus, or vertigo, so only one coherent rating construct may be used.

Primary condition: Service-connected residuals of traumatic brain injury, with a documented closed-head or blast injury and persistent physical residuals including balance or vestibular dysfunction
Primary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8045 (residuals of traumatic brain injury) — evaluated on the cognitive-impairment and subjective-symptoms table with separate evaluation of physical dysfunction under the appropriate diagnostic code; DC 8045 expressly directs that any residual with a distinct diagnosis that may be evaluated under another diagnostic code, such as migraine headache or Meniere's disease, be evaluated separately rather than under the table
Secondary condition: Meniere's disease (secondary endolymphatic hydrops) following service-connected traumatic brain injury residuals
Secondary diagnostic-code proposal: 38 CFR § 4.87, DC 6205 (Meniere's syndrome (endolymphatic hydrops)): 100 percent for hearing impairment with attacks of vertigo and cerebellar gait occurring more than once weekly; 60 percent for one to four attacks a month; 30 percent for vertigo less than once a month; with the note that the condition may instead be evaluated by separately rating vertigo as a peripheral vestibular disorder (DC 6204), hearing impairment, and tinnitus (DC 6260), whichever method yields the higher overall evaluation, but with no combining of those separate evaluations with an evaluation under DC 6205. Qualified-human rating review required
Original nexus theory: Causation

Legal boundary: § 3.310(a) concerns proximate causation; § 3.310(b) concerns attributable worsening beyond natural progression against a qualifying baseline. The at least as likely as not standard requires individual evidence and competing causes to be weighed. Apply claim-period rating criteria and § 4.14 nonpyramiding.

sourceReferences.citation: Ashley P O'Connell Ferster; Sebahattin Cureoglu; Nevra Keskin; Michael M Paparella; Huseyin Isildak. Secondary Endolymphatic Hydrops PMID 28306649.
sourceReferences.note: Review establishing secondary endolymphatic hydrops as an inner-ear pathologic finding that produces episodic vertigo and intermittent hearing loss, with post-mortem temporal-bone histopathology demonstrating hydrops plus necrotic organ of Corti in a post-traumatic case — the mechanistic source linking head trauma to hydrops.

sourceReferences.citation: Juyong Chung; Hahn Jin Jung; Chong Sun Kim; Young Ho Kim. A Case of Post-Traumatic Meniere's Disease PMID 24782951.
sourceReferences.note: Case report of post-traumatic Meniere's disease following head trauma, with tinnitus, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, and recurrent vertigo that failed symptomatic medical treatment and improved markedly only after endolymphatic sac decompression — documented human example of the trauma-to-Meniere's sequence.

sourceReferences.citation: P DiBiase; M A Arriaga. Post-traumatic hydrops PMID 9386247.
sourceReferences.note: Clinical and histopathologic analysis stating that post-traumatic Meniere's disease is a true clinical entity, that the traumatic insult may be a blow to the head or a temporal bone fracture, and simultaneously recording that many Meniere's disease cases have no identifiable etiologic agent — the etiologic-affirmation evidence together with its candid limitation.
